questions.prompt: Which best describes a design pattern?

options.text: A named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem that you adapt to your situation
A snippet of code you copy and paste unchanged
A library you install from npm

questions.explanation: A pattern is a general, reusable solution you adapt — not copy-paste code, not a library, and not an algorithm (which computes a result rather than arranging responsibilities).

questions.prompt: Match each GoF category to what it is mainly about.
questions.explanation: GoF sorts the 23 patterns into creational (how objects are made), structural (how they're assembled), and behavioral (how they interact).

questions.prompt: Which statements about design patterns are TRUE? Select all that apply.

options.text: They give a team a shared vocabulary for design
They always make code better, so use as many as possible
They come with consequences and trade-offs
They describe an arrangement you adapt, not exact code

questions.explanation: Patterns are a shared vocabulary, carry trade-offs, and are adaptable templates. Applying as many as possible is over-engineering — patterns are not a quality badge.

questions.prompt: Complete the GoF principle: "Program to an ____, not an implementation."
questions.explanation: Depending on an interface (what an object can do) rather than a concrete class (how it does it) lets you swap implementations freely.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many patterns did the Gang of Four catalog, and in what year?
questions.explanation: The 1994 GoF book cataloged 23 patterns. (Christopher Alexander's architectural book that inspired the idea was 1977.)

questions.prompt: A developer wraps a one-line config read in three interfaces, an Abstract Factory, and a Singleton 'to be enterprise-ready.' What is this an example of?

options.text: Over-engineering — paying a pattern's cost with no matching benefit

questions.explanation: Patterns add classes and indirection. Applying them where simple code would do adds cost with no benefit — the definition of over-engineering.
